evidence.claim: The Brandywine Valley Scenic Byway links wooded roads, fields and creek crossings in southeastern Pennsylvania.
evidence.quote: Near Longwood Gardens, PA 52 splits from US 1 by heading north on two-lane undivided Lenape Road. The road runs a short distance east of the border between East Marlborough Township to the west and Pennsbury Township to the east as it passes through a mix of woods and fields

evidence.claim: PennDOT designated its corridor along PA 52, PA 162 and Old Creek Road in 2005.
evidence.quote: BRANDYWINE VALLEY SCENIC BYWAY Effective: 2005 District: 6-0 County: Chester State Route: 0052 and 0162 Route 52, 0162 and Old Creek Road (Old PA Route 100).

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration identifies commerce, agriculture, artistic creativity and political thought as defining strands of the valley, and notes structures associated with the Underground Railroad along the byway.
evidence.quote: The Brandywine Valley Scenic Byway winds through the Brandywine Valley, known for its strategic crossroads of commerce, agriculture, artistic creativity, and political thought. Evidence of the settlement and development patterns can be found throughout the lands that the byway traverses. In addition, many structures that held meaning during the time of the Underground Railroad are located along the byway.

evidence.claim: The road numbers came long after some of the routes they mark.
evidence.quote: The portion of road between Marshallton and West Chester follows the 17th-century Great Minquas Path and became part of the Strasburg Road linking Strasburg and Philadelphia in the 1770s.

evidence.claim: Between Marshallton and West Chester, part of PA 162 follows the Great Minquas Path and became part of Strasburg Road in the 1770s.
evidence.quote: The portion of road between Marshallton and West Chester follows the 17th-century Great Minquas Path and became part of the Strasburg Road linking Strasburg and Philadelphia in the 1770s.

evidence.claim: PA 52 changed again in 2011, when a new alignment opened north of US 1 to improve traffic flow; part of the former road became an entrance road for Longwood Gardens.
evidence.quote: In 2010, construction began to relocate PA 52 onto a new alignment between US 1 and PA 926 in order to improve traffic flow. This shortened but did not eliminate the wrong-way concurrency between US 1 and PA 52. The new alignment of PA 52 opened on October 25, 2011 at a cost of $15.4 million. With completion of the new alignment, the former PA 52 south of Webb Barn Lane became an access road to Longwood Gardens

evidence.claim: Coming north from Delaware, Kennett Pike passes through wooded residential country before joining US 1 at Hamorton.
evidence.quote: From the state line, the route heads north-northwest on two-lane undivided Kennett Pike through wooded residential areas. The road enters Kennett Township and heads northwest to the community of Mendenhall, where it crosses an East Penn Railroad line at-grade. Farther northwest, PA 52 comes to an intersection with US 1 (Baltimore Pike) in the community of Hamorton and turns west to form a concurrency with that route

evidence.claim: PA 52 leaves US 1 near Longwood Gardens, winds toward Lenape and crosses the Brandywine on Lenape Bridge.
evidence.quote: In the community of Lenape, PA 52 heads across another East Penn Railroad line at-grade prior to crossing the Brandywine Creek and then over a parking lot on the Lenape Bridge

evidence.claim: It then follows Creek Road briefly before continuing along Lenape Road toward West Chester.
evidence.quote: Here, the road turns northwest onto Creek Road (the old alignment of PA 100) prior to continuing northeast along Lenape Road into East Bradford Township.

evidence.claim: The PA 162 branch approaches the borough from the west along Strasburg Road.
evidence.quote: At this point, the route turns east, following Strasburg Road to US 322 Bus. in West Chester.

evidence.claim: Longwood began with trees threatened by timber cutting.
evidence.quote: a lumber mill operator was about to cut down the trees for timber in early 1906.

evidence.claim: Samuel and Joshua Peirce began planting an arboretum on their inherited farm in 1798.
evidence.quote: In 1798, Joshua's twin grandsons Samuel and Joshua, who had inherited the farm, actively pursued an interest in natural history and began planting an arboretum

evidence.claim: When a lumber operator prepared to fell the trees in 1906, Pierre S. du Pont bought the property primarily to preserve them.
evidence.quote: a lumber mill operator was about to cut down the trees for timber in early 1906. This threat moved Pierre S. du Pont, American entrepreneur, businessman, philanthropist, and member of the du Pont family, to take action. On July 20, 1906, 36-year-old du Pont purchased the farm primarily to preserve the trees

evidence.claim: He added the Flower Garden Walk in 1907 and opened the garden to the public in 1921.
evidence.quote: he began developing the outdoor gardens further, adding the 600-foot long Flower Garden Walk in 1907.

evidence.claim: Peirce’s Park remains part of the gardens, with the Sylvan Fountain that du Pont added in 1925–27.
evidence.quote: Visitors to Longwood Gardens today still enjoy Peirce's Park, which is now punctuated by the Sylvan Fountain, added by Pierre S. du Pont in 1925–27.

evidence.claim: The enlarged brick farmhouse built by Joshua Peirce in 1730 also survives.
evidence.quote: in 1730 he built the brick farmhouse that, enlarged, still stands today.

evidence.claim: He added the Flower Garden Walk in 1907 and opened the garden to the public in 1921.

evidence.claim: Built in 1911–1912 from random rubble stone, the bridge has seven arches, each spanning 44 feet.
evidence.quote: It has a seven spans, each 44-foot-long (13 m), with a total length of 308-foot (94 m).  The bridge was constructed in 1911–1912, of random rubble stone.

evidence.claim: The whole structure measures 308 feet.
evidence.quote: with a total length of 308-foot (94 m).

evidence.quote: Lenape is centered on the intersection of Pennsylvania Route 52 and Pocopson Road, west of the Brandywine Creek.

evidence.claim: Construction was completed under the government of independent Pennsylvania.
evidence.quote: This road was completed under a new administration of an independent state of Pennsylvania.
